title: Jonah and the Portrait
premise: Marguerite Eriksen, a property surveyor sent to appraise the decaying Voss house in the village of Hollowmere, discovers a portrait in the attic that seems to appraise her back — and the village church bell, melted down in 1911, begins to ring each dusk. The portrait is the last of the Voss line, sustained by a count of souls owed at every harvest moon, and the villagers' loyalty to an old bargain keeps them feeding it names. Marguerite must convince the last family tied to the house — the skeptical, complicit Aldous Voss and his daughter — to leave before the moon rises and the count closes. In the end Marguerite burns the portrait, but the final page reveals her own face has begun appearing in its canvas, painted by no hand.
about_author: Theo Almeida is the pen name of a former land registry clerk from coastal Maine who spent a decade cataloguing houses that refused to sell. Their fiction draws on appraisal reports, probate disputes, and the quiet dread of buildings that remember their owners.

chapters.title: The Appraisal
chapters.summary: Marguerite's POV. She arrives at the Voss house with a clipboard and a firm disbelief in anything unmeasurable, noting sagging joists, cold rooms, and a portrait in the attic whose eyes follow her clipboard as she writes. The emotional beat: professional detachment beginning to crack at the edges.

chapters.title: A Bell That Wasn't There
chapters.summary: Marguerite's POV. At dusk the church bell rings — but the vicar shows her the 1911 ledger recording it was melted for scrap. The villagers hear nothing, or pretend to. She meets Aldous Voss, who begs her to finish quickly and leave. Beat: unease sharpening into dread.

chapters.title: The Family That Stays
chapters.summary: Aldous's POV. He explains, obliquely, that his family has never been permitted to leave: deeds signed in blood-ink, ancestors who tried and were found back at the gate each morning. His daughter Wren wants out. Beat: loyalty to a cursed inheritance versus a father's buried guilt.

chapters.title: What the Portrait Wants
chapters.summary: Marguerite's POV. She photographs the portrait; the prints develop wrong, showing the figure closer each time. Research in the parish archive reveals a pattern of surveyors who came before her — all listed as having 'remained.' Beat: the horror becomes personal and statistical.

chapters.title: The Count
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Wren reveals the family secret: every harvest moon the portrait counts the souls bound to the house, and anyone who knows its face when the bell rings thirteen times is added. Her mother was counted eleven years ago. Beat: terror mixed with defiant hope.

chapters.title: Villagers
chapters.summary: Marguerite's POV. She tries to rally the village and meets smiling stonewalls — the town's prosperity, she realizes, is bought with the occasional missing outsider. The innkeeper warns her gently to stop asking. Beat: isolation; the corruption of collective complicity.

chapters.title: Aldous Breaks
chapters.summary: Aldous's POV. Aldous attempts to burn the portrait himself and cannot — his hands turn the match aside against his will, the bargain overriding his body. Marguerite catches him weeping in the hall. Beat: the crushing weight of inherited power and failed courage.

chapters.title: Thirteen Rings
chapters.summary: Marguerite's POV. Two nights before the harvest moon, the bell rings thirteen times early — a test, or a trap. A villager who helped her is found inside the portrait's frame, newly painted. Beat: grief, and the certainty that there will be no second chances.

chapters.title: The Harvest Moon
chapters.summary: Multiple POVs converging. Marguerite smuggles Aldous and Wren out through the cellar while the bell tolls and the portrait's count climbs aloud like an auctioneer. At the gate the road folds back on itself until Marguerite turns and faces the painting directly, refusing to look away. Beat: climax — truth stared down over loyalty to any bargain.

chapters.title: Sold
chapters.summary: Marguerite's POV, weeks later. The house burns; the Vosses settle in a coastal town; the bell never rings again. Marguerite files her final report, then unwraps a canvas she took as evidence — and finds her own portrait half-finished, one brushstroke more each morning. Beat: resolution with a slow, patient horror.
